section: Chapter 5 Review Questions ▷ Counterexamples to Scalar Rules

A real 2 × 2 matrix satisfies A = I and tr A = 0. What is det A?
(A) −2 (B) −1 (C) 0 (D) 1 (E) 2

solution.text:
2
Eigenvalues of an involution satisfy λ = 1. Trace zero forces one 1 and one −1, so the de-
2
terminant is −1. Alternatively Cayley–Hamilton gives A + (det A)I = 0, hence det A = −1.

A nilpotent linear operator on R has rank four. What is its nilpotency index?
(A) 1 (B) 2 (C) 3 (D) 4 (E) 5

solution.text:
k k+1
The kernel has dimension one. For each k, restriction of N maps ker N into ker N with
k
kernel ker N , so the kernel dimensions can increase by at most one per power. To reach
dimension five therefore requires at least five powers. Cayley–Hamilton bounds the index
by five, giving exactly five.

(A) N + M is nilpotent. (B) N + M is involutory.
(C) N M = M N. (D) NM = 0.
(E) N is invertible.

solution.text:
2 2 2
Both N and M are zero, but NM = diag(1, 0) and MN = diag(0, 1). Hence (N + M) =
NM + MN = I. A sum of nilpotents need not be nilpotent, because the factors need not
commute.
